Rasch Partial Credit Model with easyRaschBayes

Source: vignettes/pcm-rasch-analysis.Rmd
pcm-rasch-analysis.Rmd

Overview

This vignette shows a Rasch analysis of a polytomous questionnaire with easyRaschBayes, using the partial credit model (PCM) fitted with brms. The data are the PHQ-9 depression screener, included in the package as phq9.

The functions work with Bayesian Rasch models fitted with brms: the partial credit model (acat family with thres(gr = item)), the rating scale model, the dichotomous Rasch model (bernoulli family), and a hurdle partial credit model for data with many zero responses (see the hurdle PCM vignette). A code example for the dichotomous model is available here, and more detail on Rasch models in brms is in Bürkner (2021).

The frequentist counterpart is easyRasch2, which uses conditional maximum likelihood and simulation-based critical values. Its Get Started vignette analyses the same phq9 data, so the two can be read side by side. Several functions here follow their easyRasch2 counterparts, for example plot_icc() (RMitemICCPlot()) and plot_targeting() (RMtargeting()). Each function has documentation and example code, see ?function_name.

The sections follow the four requirements of a Rasch model (Christensen et al. 2013; Christensen et al. 2021):

  1. Unidimensionality — the items measure a single latent variable.
  2. Local independence — given the latent variable, item responses are independent of each other.
  3. Ordered response categories — moving up the latent variable increases the probability of higher categories.
  4. Invariance (no differential item functioning) — item parameters are the same across relevant groups, here gender.

They are followed by descriptors that are usually reported alongside the four requirements:

  • Targeting — how well person and item locations overlap on the latent variable.
  • Reliability — how precisely the scale separates respondents.
  • Item and person parameters — item thresholds, person locations, and a table from sum score to person location.
library(easyRaschBayes)
library(brms)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)

Data

phq9 holds 600 respondents to the PHQ-9 (Kroenke et al. 2001) in the U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES, September 2024 release), with complete responses on all nine items. Respondents with a sum score of zero were reduced by hand, so symptom levels are much higher than in the NHANES population. See ?phq9, and the phq9_nhanes data for a random sample. Each item is scored 0 (“Not at all”), 1 (“Several days”), 2 (“More than half the days”) and 3 (“Nearly every day”).

data(phq9)
items <- phq9[, 1:9]

item_desc <- c(
  q1 = "Little interest or pleasure in doing things",
  q2 = "Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless",
  q3 = "Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much",
  q4 = "Feeling tired or having little energy",
  q5 = "Poor appetite or overeating",
  q6 = "Feeling bad about yourself, or that you are a failure",
  q7 = "Trouble concentrating on things",
  q8 = "Moving or speaking slowly, or being fidgety or restless",
  q9 = "Thoughts that you would be better off dead, or of hurting yourself"
)
resp_labels <- c("Not at all", "Several days", "More than half the days",
                 "Nearly every day")

summary(rowSums(items))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    0.00   10.00   16.00   15.41   21.00   27.00
table(phq9$gender, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#> Female   Male   <NA> 
#>    426    143     31
item description

Descriptive plots

Before fitting a model it is good to look at the response distributions. The plotting functions take wide data, one column per item.

plot_stackedbars(items)

Figure 1. Response distribution per item

plot_tile() and plot_bars() show the same data in other forms.

Long format

brms needs long data, one row per person and item. The acat family expects response categories starting at 1, so we add 1 to every response. The functions in this package score the responses from 0 again in their output.

df_pcm <- phq9 %>%
  rownames_to_column("id") %>%
  select(id, gender, starts_with("q")) %>%
  pivot_longer(starts_with("q"), names_to = "item",
               values_to = "response") %>%
  mutate(response = response + 1)

head(df_pcm)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   id    gender item  response
#>   <chr> <fct>  <chr>    <dbl>
#> 1 1     Female q1           4
#> 2 1     Female q2           4
#> 3 1     Female q3           4
#> 4 1     Female q4           4
#> 5 1     Female q5           4
#> 6 1     Female q6           4

Fitting the PCM

The model is fitted once and saved. The chunk below shows the call, which is not run when the vignette is built. The saved model is loaded instead.

prior_pcm <- prior("normal(0, 3)", class = "Intercept") +
  prior("normal(0, 3)", class = "sd", group = "id")
fit_pcm <- brm(
  response | thres(gr = item) ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  data   = df_pcm,
  family = acat,
  prior  = prior_pcm,
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000
)
saveRDS(fit_pcm, "fits/fit_pcm_phq9.rds")
fit_pcm <- readRDS("fits/fit_pcm_phq9.rds")

thres(gr = item) gives each item its own thresholds, which makes this a partial credit model. (1 | id) is the person location.

For a rating scale model, where all items share the same distances between thresholds and differ only in location, drop thres(gr = item) and add an item effect instead. The thresholds are then common to all items, and each item’s location is shifted by its coefficient:

fit_rsm <- brm(
  response ~ 1 + item + (1 | id),
  data   = df_pcm,
  family = acat,
  prior  = prior("normal(0, 3)", class = "Intercept") +
    prior("normal(0, 3)", class = "b") +
    prior("normal(0, 3)", class = "sd", group = "id"),
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 2000
)

The functions in this package accept this model in the same way. loo_compare() can then be used to compare it with the partial credit model.

1. Unidimensionality

Item fit: conditional infit

infit_statistic() computes infit (and optionally outfit, see Müller (2020)) mean squares for each item, conditional on each person’s total score, as in iarm::out_infit(). For the same item parameters the observed values are the same as iarm’s. The function compares them with data replicated from the model, also conditional on the total score.

The ndraws_use argument limits the number of posterior draws used, which makes exploration faster. For final results, use all draws (ndraws_use = NULL, the default).

fit_stats <- infit_statistic(fit_pcm, ndraws_use = 500)

infit_results <- infit_post(fit_stats)
infit_results$summary
#> # A tibble: 9 × 4
#>   item  infit_obs infit_rep infit_ppp
#>   <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 q1        0.95      1.00      0.162
#> 2 q2        0.784     0.998     0    
#> 3 q3        1.24      1         1    
#> 4 q4        0.833     1         0.01 
#> 5 q5        1.08      0.999     0.88 
#> 6 q6        0.904     1.00      0.056
#> 7 q7        0.995     1         0.48 
#> 8 q8        1.27      1.00      0.998
#> 9 q9        1.33      1.00      1
infit_results$plot

Figure 2. Observed and replicated infit

infit_obs is the observed infit and infit_rep the infit of replicated data. Values above 1 mean more variation in the responses than the model expects (underfit), which can indicate multidimensionality. Values below 1 mean less (overfit), which can come with local dependence. infit_ppp is the proportion of posterior draws where the observed infit exceeds the replicated one. Values near 0.5 indicate good fit, values near 1 underfit, and values near 0 overfit.

The ppp is conservative, because the item parameters are estimated from the same data. In simulations under a fitting model it rarely came close to 0 or 1, so misfit can go undetected. We therefore also use the item-restscore association below, whose ppp was close to uniform in the same simulations. The ppp is not a measure of the size of misfit.

Three items underfit: q9 (thoughts of self-harm, infit about 1.33), q8 (moving slowly or restless, 1.27) and q3 (sleep, 1.24), all with infit_ppp near 1. Two overfit: q2 (feeling down, 0.78) and q4 (feeling tired, 0.83). Given how conservative the ppp is, values this close to 0 or 1 are clear signals, but they should not be read item by item. Infit is relative to the other items. An item in a strongly dependent pair usually overfits, and that makes the remaining items look more underfit than they would otherwise. q2 is part of the strongest dependent pair (see local dependence below), so fit should be checked again after the dependence is dealt with, for example by removing one item of the pair.

Item-restscore association

item_restscore_statistic() computes Goodman-Kruskal’s gamma between each item and the rest score (the total score minus the item), and compares it with the gamma expected under the model given the total scores (Kreiner 2011). The expected value differs between items, since it depends on item locations and targeting. An observed gamma above the expected value means the item discriminates more than the model implies, and below it less. ppp is a posterior predictive p-value from data replicated conditional on each person’s total score. Values near 1 mean a stronger association than expected, and near 0 a weaker one. p_adj is two-sided and adjusted for the number of items, so small values flag a departure in either direction.

rest_stats <- item_restscore_statistic(fit_pcm, ndraws_use = 500)

rest_results <- item_restscore_post(rest_stats)
rest_results$summary
#> # A tibble: 9 × 6
#>   item  gamma_obs gamma_exp gamma_diff   ppp p_adj
#>   <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 q1        0.658     0.62       0.039 0.938 0.7  
#> 2 q2        0.725     0.624      0.101 1     0    
#> 3 q3        0.569     0.629     -0.06  0     0.048
#> 4 q4        0.712     0.617      0.095 1     0    
#> 5 q5        0.62      0.623     -0.003 0.392 1    
#> 6 q6        0.69      0.627      0.063 0.992 0.058
#> 7 q7        0.642     0.624      0.019 0.774 0.996
#> 8 q8        0.55      0.635     -0.085 0     0    
#> 9 q9        0.59      0.638     -0.048 0.02  0.25
rest_results$plot

Figure 3. Observed and expected item-restscore gamma

Item-restscore agrees with infit for four of the five items. q2 and q4 have a stronger association with the rest score than expected (p_adj near 0), and q8 and q3 a weaker one. q9 has a weaker association than expected as well (ppp 0.02), but after adjustment for the number of items it is not flagged (p_adj 0.25). q6 leans towards overfit (ppp 0.99, p_adj 0.06).

Conditional item characteristic curves

plot_icc() compares the model-expected item score with the observed mean item score in class intervals of the total score. Persons with the minimum or maximum total score are left out. By default the respondents are split into class_intervals = 5 groups of about equal size (method = "quantile"). Other options are equal-width groups ("width"), one group per total score ("score"), or groups set by hand ("manual" with score_breaks). Tied total scores can give fewer quantile groups than requested, and the caption states the grouping that was used.

plot_icc(fit_pcm)

Figure 4. Conditional item characteristic curves

The curves show the same items. The observed points of q8 and q9 are flatter than the model curve, above it in the middle and below it at the top, which is what underfit looks like. q2 and q4 are slightly steeper than the curve.

Residual PCA

plot_residual_pca() runs a principal components analysis of the person-item residuals and plots the loadings on the first residual contrast against the item locations, with the uncertainty of both.

pca <- plot_residual_pca(fit_pcm, ndraws_use = 500)
pca$eigenvalue
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   eigenvalue_obs eigenvalue_rep eigenvalue_diff   ppp var_explained_obs
#>            <dbl>          <dbl>           <dbl> <dbl>             <dbl>
#> 1           1.66           1.24           0.424     1             0.181
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: var_explained_rep <dbl>
pca$plot

Figure 5. Loadings on the first residual contrast and item locations

ppp in pca$eigenvalue is the proportion of draws where the observed largest eigenvalue exceeds the replicated one. Values near 1 suggest more structure in the residuals than the model implies. Items with loadings of opposite sign on the first contrast are candidates for a second dimension.

The observed first eigenvalue (1.66) is larger than the replicated one (1.24) in every draw. The loadings separate q3, q5 and q4 (sleep, appetite and tiredness) from q9, q2, q6 and q1 (self-harm thoughts, feeling down, feeling bad about yourself and little interest). The somatic items share something the model does not capture, and so do the mood items.

2. Local independence

q3_statistic() computes Yen’s Q3 (Yen 1984), the correlation between the residuals of each pair of items. Given the latent variable, residuals should be uncorrelated, and pairs with higher correlations than the model replicates suggest local dependence (Levy et al. 2009). As for infit and item-restscore, the residuals are taken from the expected responses given each person’s total score. Given the total score, a person’s residuals sum to zero, so Q3 centres on about -1/(k-1), here -0.125, rather than on 0 (Christensen et al. 2017). The replicated values have the same centre, so q3_diff (observed minus replicated) is the quantity to read. q3_ppp near 1 flags a pair, and q3_p_adj adjusts for the 36 pairs, with small values flagging a pair. The dashed line in the plot is the mean replicated Q3.

q3_stats <- q3_statistic(fit_pcm, ndraws_use = 500)

q3_results <- q3_post(q3_stats)
q3_results$summary
#> # A tibble: 36 × 8
#>    item_pair item_1 item_2 q3_obs q3_rep q3_diff q3_ppp q3_p_adj
#>    <chr>     <chr>  <chr>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1 q1 : q2   q1     q2      0.239 -0.121   0.361  1        0    
#>  2 q3 : q5   q3     q5      0.075 -0.139   0.214  1        0    
#>  3 q3 : q4   q3     q4      0.062 -0.128   0.19   1        0    
#>  4 q7 : q8   q7     q8      0.066 -0.115   0.181  1        0    
#>  5 q2 : q9   q2     q9      0.049 -0.123   0.171  1        0    
#>  6 q2 : q6   q2     q6      0.016 -0.132   0.148  1        0.006
#>  7 q4 : q5   q4     q5     -0.01  -0.123   0.113  0.996    0.11 
#>  8 q6 : q9   q6     q9     -0.003 -0.115   0.112  1        0.072
#>  9 q8 : q9   q8     q9     -0.109 -0.196   0.086  0.958    0.744
#> 10 q1 : q4   q1     q4     -0.023 -0.105   0.082  0.984    0.568
#> # ℹ 26 more rows
q3_results$plot

Figure 6. Q3 residual correlations

In the plot, the grey distributions are the replicated Q3 and the points are the observed Q3. The observed values vary little across draws, because the residuals given the total score depend only on the item parameters, which 600 persons estimate precisely. The replicated values also vary through the sampling of new responses, so they are wider. Each pair has its own expected value, so the grey distributions are not all centred on the dashed line.

The largest difference by far is for q1 and q2, the two core symptoms of depression (little interest and feeling down), with an observed Q3 of 0.24 against about -0.12 replicated. Next, with differences of about 0.15 to 0.2, are q3 with q5 and with q4, q7 with q8, q2 with q9, and q2 with q6. All six have q3_p_adj below .05, and they match the two groups in the residual PCA. q4 with q5 and q6 with q9 follow at about 0.11, with q3_ppp near 1 but q3_p_adj above .05.

Pairs with lower residual correlations than replicated are also worth a look. When items form two groups, items within a group have residual correlations above the replicated ones and items from different groups below. Here the lowest pairs, about 0.12 to 0.21 below the replicated values, are mostly one somatic and one mood item: q4 with q9, q2 with q8, q2 with q5, q5 with q9 and q3 with q9. Together with the positive pairs and the residual PCA, this points to a somatic and a mood dimension rather than to dependence between single pairs of items.

3. Ordered response categories

plot_ipf() shows the probability of each response category across the latent variable, with the uncertainty as a shaded band. Where two adjacent curves cross is the threshold between them. A category whose curve is never the highest is never the most likely response at any location.

plot_ipf(fit_pcm, theta_range = c(-5, 5))

Figure 7. Item category probability functions

item_parameters() reports the thresholds, and whether they are in order:

ipar <- item_parameters(fit_pcm)
knitr::kable(ipar$locations_wide, digits = 2)

q7 -1.27 0.02 0.54 -0.24
q5 -1.09 -0.07 0.68 -0.16
q1 -1.95 0.62 0.96 -0.12
q9 0.74 1.63 1.31 1.23
q8 0.90 1.60 1.71 1.40 
ipar$threshold_order
#> # A tibble: 9 × 4
#>   item  n_thresholds ordered prob_disordered
#>   <chr>        <int> <lgl>             <dbl>
#> 1 q1               3 TRUE             0.0525
#> 2 q2               3 TRUE             0.125 
#> 3 q3               3 TRUE             0.162 
#> 4 q4               3 TRUE             0.0118
#> 5 q5               3 TRUE             0

#> 9 q9               3 FALSE            0.880

The thresholds are in order for all items except q9, where the posterior probability that they are disordered is 0.88. Thresholds 2 and 3 of q9 are disordered, so “More than half the days” is never the most likely response to that item. Together with q8, it is the item fewest people endorse at all.

4. Invariance: differential item functioning

dif_statistic() refits the model with item-specific differences between two groups, here women and men, and summarises the posterior of each item’s DIF. A difference in the latent means of the groups (impact) is estimated separately. DIF is defined relative to the average item, so it sums to about zero across items, and positive DIF means the item is easier for the second group (here "Male") at the same latent level. The 31 respondents without gender are left out.

df_dif <- df_pcm %>% filter(!is.na(gender))

dif <- dif_statistic(fit_pcm, group_var = gender, data = df_dif, rope = 0,
                     cores = 4, refresh = 0, seed = 2024)
saveRDS(dif, "fits/dif_gender_phq9.rds")

The DIF model takes a few minutes to fit, so as for the main model, the saved result is loaded here.

dif <- readRDS("fits/dif_gender_phq9.rds")
dif$impact
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   estimate    sd  lower upper
#>      <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1   0.0816 0.174 -0.260 0.418
dif$summary
#> # A tibble: 9 × 8
#>   item  dif_estimate dif_sd dif_lower dif_upper    pd rope_percentage flag      
#>   <chr>        <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>           <dbl> <chr>

dif$plot

Figure 8. DIF by gender

rope = 0 reports the posteriors without a region of practical equivalence. Whether a DIF of a given size matters depends on how the scores are used, for example through its effect on person locations, so there is no general cut-off.

The conditional item characteristic curves can be split by group, with the partial gamma for each item, which measures the association between item response and group within total-score strata:

plot_icc(fit_pcm, dif_var = gender, dif_data = df_pcm)

Figure 9. Conditional ICCs by gender

The difference in latent means between men and women (impact) is small and uncertain, about 0.08 logits with an interval from -0.26 to 0.42. The largest DIF is for q2 (feeling down), about 0.3 logits easier for men: at the same overall level of depression, men report feeling down more often than women. q5 (appetite) is harder for men by about the same amount, and q9 easier by a little less. For these three items the probability of direction is about 0.97, so the sign is fairly certain, while the size is not: the intervals are about 0.6 logits wide. The partial gamma in the curves points the same way (0.41 for q2, -0.29 for q5). Whether differences of this size matter can be judged by their effect on the person locations, for example by comparing the persons’ locations with and without the items.

Targeting

plot_targeting() shows person locations above the item thresholds on the same logit scale. The top panel is the distribution of person locations (EAP by default, person_estimate = "wle" for WLE). The bottom panel draws each item as a bar split into the ranges where each response category is the most likely response, with the threshold credible intervals below. A category that is never the most likely response, or disordered thresholds, are marked in red with the posterior probability of that. panel = "thresholds" gives a simpler threshold plot.

plot_targeting(fit_pcm, category_labels = resp_labels)

Figure 10. Person-item targeting

The person locations (mean 0.45, SD 1.23) overlap the thresholds well. This sample was selected to have few respondents without symptoms, see ?phq9. The two hardest items, q8 and q9, are located above most persons. On q9, category 2 collapses, as found above, and the arrow gives the distance between the disordered thresholds and the probability that the category is never the most likely response.

Reliability

RMUreliability() gives a Bayesian reliability estimate based on relative measurement uncertainty (RMU, Bignardi et al. 2026). It takes a matrix of person location draws, persons by draws, and returns the posterior mean with a 95% highest density continuous interval.

person_draws <- fit_pcm %>%
  as_draws_df() %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(starts_with("r_id")) %>%
  t()
RMUreliability(person_draws)
#>   rmu_estimate hdci_lowerbound hdci_upperbound .width .point .interval
#> 1    0.8807332       0.8666336       0.8954398   0.95   mean      hdci

RMU ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values meaning more reliable person locations, and can be read like other reliability coefficients. Here it is 0.88, with an interval from 0.87 to 0.90.
